title: The Marines land on Tarawa
pull: Hundreds of yards of open water, under fire

facts.text: On the morning of 20 November 1943, the 2nd Marine Division under Maj. Gen. Julian C. Smith landed on Betio, the main island of Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands. The operation was called Galvanic.
Betio was tiny: about 2 miles long, about 800 yards wide at its widest, and nowhere more than about 10 feet above the sea. The Japanese had turned it into a fortress.
The first amphibian tractors (amtracs) reached the beach at 9:10 a.m. on Red Beach One. Within about 10 minutes, amtracs had put more than 1,500 Marines ashore on the north coast.

A neap tide left only about 3 feet of water over the coral reef. Higgins boats needed about 4 feet, so they grounded on the reef, and the Marines in them had to wade 500 to 1,000 yards to shore under fire.
The tracked amtracs could crawl over the reef. The Marines used 125 of them at Betio, and only 35 were left at the end.
The first amtrac ashore, nicknamed "My Deloris" and driven by PFC Edward J. Moore, tried to climb a five foot seawall and stalled almost on end. Moore reached for his rifle and found it shot in half.
Organized resistance ended at 1:05 p.m. on 23 November, about 76 hours after the first amtrac hit the beach.

More than 1,000 Marines and Navy corpsmen were killed and more than 2,000 wounded. The Marine Corps history counts 3,407 casualties in all, about as many as the Marines lost in six months on Guadalcanal.
Of the island's defenders, 4,690 died. Only 17 wounded Japanese were taken prisoner, along with 129 Korean laborers.

Headlines about "The Bloody Beaches of Tarawa" shocked Americans. The hard lessons, among them more and better armored amtracs and heavier, more accurate bombardment, shaped every Pacific landing that followed.

photoNote: Marines wading toward the beach off Tarawa, rifles held up, a long line of men stretching back toward the reef, the side of a landing boat in the foreground. Original caption: "Marines Wade Ashore. Despite enemy fire Marines wade through the surf off Tarawa Island. Landing boats and barges brought them to within 500 yards of the beach but the coral bottom prevented the boats coming any closer to the shore." National Archives, Record Group 38 (Office of the Chief of Naval Operations), NAID 32606885, use Unrestricted, US government work, public domain. Cropped off the print border, 1920 x 1589. Exact day not in the caption (a companion print, NAID 32606882, says reinforcements wading in), so the credit says November 1943. Frame on the lead Marines at left and center; the boat gunwale at the bottom can be cropped.
photoCredit: Marines wade ashore through the shallows off Betio, Tarawa, November 1943. National Archives 32606885, public domain.

declassified.fact: "My Deloris" never ran again. Crews tried to salvage her during the battle, but she was too riddled with shell holes, so she was shipped home as an exhibit for War Bond drives. Today she is at the Marine Corps tracked vehicle museum at Camp Del Mar, California.

film.shot_notes: Navy color camera original behind With the Marines at Tarawa, silent, 12 min 9 s (Film Library: tarawa-navy-reels index). The opening minutes are shipboard life and the briefing on a relief map (not used; 15768 is a rehearsal). NOON: 07:12 to 08:05 Betio under bombardment, shell bursts and smoke columns, planes overhead; 08:28 to 09:45 the run in, a wave of LVTs heading for the beach through fires and shell splashes. Open on a burst or the LVTs moving. 09:45 to 11:07 (LVTs at the beach, troops ashore, amtrac 67 at 10:53) is reserved for No. 079's 7 p.m. video.
